entry.evidence: how does surface water carbonate chemistry respond to an upwelling event?

steps.action: Posed two questions: how surface carbonate chemistry responds to an upwelling event, and how OMZ waters with different chemical signatures modulate it.
steps.quote: how does surface water carbonate chemistry respond to an upwelling event?

steps.action: Designed an in situ mesocosm test. Upwelling is simulated with OMZ waters from two sites with different nutrient signatures, and the responses are compared with natural upwelling in the ambient water.
steps.quote: An upwelling event was simulated in the mesocosms by addition of OMZ waters collected from two different locations

steps.action: Set the conditions. Eight KOSMOS mesocosms were enclosed; Low DIN (70 m) and Very low DIN (30 m) OMZ waters were added to four mesocosms each on days 11-12; NaCl brine was added on days 13 and 33.
steps.quote: During the night of 8 March (day 11), ∼ 10 m 3 of OMZ water was added to 14–17 m of each mesocosm.

steps.action: Sampled surface and bottom layers of the mesocosms and the Pacific daily or every second day for 50 d. Measured TA by titration, spectrophotometric pHT, DIC (only to day 10), nutrients, and CTD profiles.
steps.quote: Depth-integrated samples were taken from the surface (0–10 m for day 3–28) and bottom layer (10–17 m for day 3–28) of the mesocosms

steps.action: Calculated in situ pCO2, DIC and calcite and aragonite saturation states from measured pHT and TA with CO2SYS, and propagated uncertainties with seacarb.
steps.quote: The observed pH T and TA as well as inorganic nutrient concentration (phosphate and silicic acid) were used as input CO 2 system parameters.

steps.action: Recorded the nutrient and chl a responses. DIN rose in Low DIN and fell in Very low DIN mesocosms and was then depleted; phosphate rose; a chl a maximum formed near 10 m.
steps.quote: The addition of OMZ water elevated surface DIN in the Low DIN mesocosms

steps.action: Compared the two treatments: OMZ addition raised surface DIC and pCO2 with no significant difference between them (Mann-Whitney U).
steps.quote: without distinct differences between the two treatments (Mann–Whitney U test, p > 0.05 ; Fig. 3c)

steps.action: Described the pCO2/DIC time series. pCO2 fell to 340-500 µatm by days 24-26, rose again, and showed anomalous trajectories in M3 (delayed decline) and M4 (persistently >700 µatm). The Pacific averaged 1078 µatm, and its bottom water was aragonite-undersaturated before day 13.
steps.quote: Interestingly, and unlike the other mesocosms, after OMZ water addition, p CO 2 in M3 steadily declined from 928 to 342 µ atm

steps.action: Estimated the Pacific air-sea CO2 flux from calculated pCO2, a wind-speed gas-transfer parameterization with GLDAS winds, and the NOAA atmospheric pCO2. The flux was 4.2-14.0 mmol C m-2 d-1 and always positive.
steps.quote: The air–sea CO 2 flux in the Pacific was constantly positive throughout our study

steps.action: Correlated the flux with its drivers: positive with wind speed (r2 = 0.4), none with temperature.
steps.quote: FCO 2 was positively correlated with near-surface wind speed ( r 2 = 0.4 ).

steps.action: Compared propagated uncertainties across the calculated variables. Saturation states are the most uncertain (5.1 %), which makes the Pacific bottom-water aragonite undersaturation ambiguous.
steps.quote: Ω Ca and Ω Ar were the most sensitive to uncertainties in pH T and TA with an average uncertainty of 5.1 %

steps.action: Checked calculated DIC (from pHT, TA) against 53 measured DIC values from days 3-10. Found r2 = 0.985 with a -8.27 µmol/kg underestimate, consistent with Raimondi et al. (2019); residuals were not correlated with inputs or temperature.
steps.quote: The calculated DIC values were generally in agreement with the measured values

steps.action: Evaluated measurement quality: pH triplicate precision, TA CRM control charts, and range charts. Found stable precision but a 17.69 µmol/kg TA accuracy offset, attributed to an unchecked titrant and corrected by CRM calibration.
steps.quote: 90.5 % of the measured TA values of CRM fell between warning limits

steps.action: Stated rival causes of the post-upwelling pCO2 decline: outgassing (possibly enhanced by El Niño warming) versus biological uptake.
steps.quote: The declining p CO 2 could be partially attributed by CO 2 outgassing

steps.action: Excluded outgassing as the sole cause, because gas exchange cannot produce undersaturation relative to the atmosphere, and because M4, with little biomass, kept high DIC.
steps.quote: However, air–sea gas exchange could not explain surface CO 2 under-saturation in relation to the atmosphere

steps.action: Kept biological uptake as the primary driver of DIC loss, while noting that the outgassing share cannot be quantified without mesocosm gas-exchange measurements.
steps.quote: strongly suggest that the loss of DIC (except M4) was primarily driven by biological uptake and phytoplankton growth

steps.action: Compared DIC drawdown between treatments: 41.0 µmol/kg higher in Low DIN (p = 0.05), but no difference in POC buildup.
steps.quote: the uptake of DIC was higher in the Low DIN mesocosms, which received more input of DIN from OMZ water addition

steps.action: Accounted for the DIC-POC mismatch with auxiliaries rather than rejecting nutrient control: small DIN contrast, A. sanguinea retaining biomass, and consumed DIC channelled to DOC (Igarza et al., 2022).
steps.quote: much of the consumed DIC could have been channeled to the dissolved organic carbon (DOC) pool

steps.action: Proposed mesocosm-specific phytoplankton succession as the cause of the post-day-24 divergence in carbonate chemistry.
steps.quote: One factor that may have controlled the differences in CO 2 increase are the mesocosm-specific phytoplankton succession patterns.

steps.action: Took the community succession record (diatoms to A. sanguinea, absent in M3 and M4) from the project's companion overview paper.
steps.quote: [...] a diatom-dominated community to a dominance of dinoflagellates (in particular Akashiwo sanguinea) occurred when DIN was exhausted

steps.action: Matched the M3 pCO2 delay with delayed chl a and reduced A. sanguinea, and the M4 high pCO2 with no bloom and no A. sanguinea.
steps.quote: M4 was the only mesocosm where A. sanguinea remained undetectable, whereas a delayed and reduced contribution by A. sanguinea was observed in M3.

steps.action: Kept A. sanguinea as a key driver of the mesocosm carbonate chemistry trends.
steps.quote: [...] that A. sanguinea was a key factor driving the trend of carbonate chemistry in the mesocosms.

steps.action: Proposed that the late second surface bloom and pCO2 decline were fuelled by Inca tern excrement.
steps.quote: This bloom was likely fueled by surface eutrophication due to defecating sea birds.

steps.action: Derived from the known composition of droppings (uric acid, ammonium) that they should acidify surface water and lower alkalinity.
steps.quote: Therefore, the droppings may lower the pH of the surface water.

steps.action: Compared with the data: no alkalinity decrease was seen, while DON rose from day 38 (Igarza et al., 2022) and chl a accumulated above the mixed layer.
steps.quote: However, this should have been visible in decreasing alkalinity, which was not the case.

steps.action: Checked mesocosm artifacts. The salinity offset from the Pacific was below 1; cited work finds brine effects negligible (Czerny 2013a) and mixing effects minor (Striebel 2013). The authors acknowledge there were no control mesocosms.
steps.quote: The difference in salinity in the mesocosms from the Pacific was less than 1 throughout the study

steps.action: Compared Pacific fluxes with Takahashi et al. (2009), the high-flux criterion of Paulmier et al. (2008), and Friederich et al. (2008). The site was a strong source, slightly higher than Friederich, explained by nearshore versus 0-200 km averaging.
steps.quote: our study site was a strong CO 2 source to the atmosphere most of the time

steps.action: Compared an upper-bound 10-d outgassing loss (0.142 mol m-2) with mesocosm DIC drawdown (1.18-1.60 mol m-2) over a 10 m column.
steps.quote: This shows that biological processes drawing down CO 2 are stronger than loss by air–sea gas exchange.

steps.action: Set the fluxes against El Niño flux reductions reported for the equatorial Pacific (Feely et al., 1999, 2002), and concluded that the size of the coastal El Niño influence cannot be determined.
steps.quote: it is difficult to conclude the magnitude of the coastal El Niño influence on the local CO 2 fluxes in our study

steps.action: Kept aragonite undersaturation in the Pacific subsurface and in the OMZ source waters as indicating a dissolution risk for calcifiers.
steps.quote: our observations of aragonite under-saturation in the Pacific suggest a potential risk of dissolution for marine calcifiers

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Natural upwelling events repeat in the Pacific; single El Niño event
Instrument QC and DIC consistency only; no control mesocosms
Biological drawdown kept as best explanation; El Niño influence unresolved

end.claim: Simulated upwelling with CO2-rich OMZ water raised mesocosm surface pCO2 above 900 µatm, after which pCO2 fell to near or below atmospheric levels mainly through phytoplankton uptake, while the ambient Pacific stayed a CO2 source of 4.2-14.0 mmol C m-2 d-1.

decisive_move.sentence: Adding two OMZ water masses to the enclosed mesocosms created the simulated upwelling, without which no response, treatment contrast, or biological drawdown could be read.

gates.evidence: The treatment design (two OMZ waters with different DIN) followed a stated research question, not a stated hypothesis (§1 ¶4). The biological-drawdown claim faced a test it could have failed: undersaturation that gas exchange cannot produce, plus the M4 low-biomass contrast (§4.2 ¶2). The bird hypothesis was checked against alkalinity (§4.2 ¶4). The A. sanguinea and El Niño interpretations are post hoc. No hypothesis, analysis, or threshold is reported as fixed before the data.

imports.item: Spectrophotometric pH with m-cresol purple indicator dye
Two-stage potentiometric titration with non-linear Gran fit
LI-COR LI-7000 infrared gas analyzer (AIRICA) for DIC
Control and range charts with warning and control limits

novelty_claims.quote: This provides first insights into how inorganic C cycling links to chemical signatures of OMZ waters in a natural plankton community
our observations can serve as the first evidence of carbonate chemistry dynamics in the coastal Peruvian upwelling system during a coastal El Niño event
our study characterized carbonate chemistry in nearshore Pacific waters that are rarely sampled in such a temporal resolution
As a unique dataset that characterized nearshore carbonate chemistry with a high temporal resolution during a rare coastal El Niño event

limits:
**Sub-claim statuses**
- Pacific flux range: estimate_with_resolution, but no flux uncertainty is reported.
- Higher DIC drawdown in Low DIN: kept at p = 0.05, with no POC difference.
- A. sanguinea as key driver: best_explanation.
- Seabird excrement causing the second bloom: best_explanation.
- Aragonite undersaturation: ambiguous given the 5.1 % uncertainty.
- El Niño influence on fluxes: no conclusion.

**Composition**
none_fits, because the walk mixes a designed manipulation without control mesocosms, monitoring of found conditions in the Pacific, and post hoc explanations. No crucial test separates the rivals.

**Evidence taken from companion work**
The succession and A. sanguinea data come from the companion paper Bach et al. (2020a), so the step is coded inherited. The DOC and DON evidence comes from Igarza et al. (2022, in preparation). Neither is shown here.

**Gaps in the measurements**
- Measured DIC exists only to day 10, so later DIC is entirely calculated.
- Mesocosm gas exchange was not measured, so the outgassing share and the C budget are unquantified.
- The TA accuracy offset (17.69 µmol/kg) is handled by CRM correction. Its effect on derived pCO2 is not reported.

**Process**
No review file or discussion was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. Inference: the published Discussion may reflect referee-driven additions (e.g., the paragraph on the lack of control mesocosms), but this cannot be established from the paper alone.

disagreements.support: Nearshore fluxes are slightly higher than the 0-200 km averaged values, explained by lower offshore pCO2 in the averaging domain.
disagreements.quote: [...] air–sea CO 2 fluxes were slightly higher than observations by Friederich et al. (2008) along the coast of Peru

disagreements.target: Position that the Peruvian upwelling region is a year-round CO2 source (Friederich et al., 2008)
disagreements.support: Mesocosm DIC drawdown after simulated upwelling exceeded the upper-bound outgassing by about an order of magnitude and drove pCO2 below atmospheric levels.
disagreements.quote: biological responses that draw down DIC can quickly turn a CO 2 source into a sink in the upwelling system

alternatives_considered.chosen: pHT and TA as input pair for carbonate speciation
alternatives_considered.reason: AIRICA DIC system malfunctioned after day 10
the repeat SD covers only random error; no pH CRM exists for systematic error

alternatives_considered.chosen: propagation of pHT and TA uncertainties only
alternatives_considered.alternatives: including nutrient, salinity and temperature input uncertainties
alternatives_considered.reason: their contributions are often small (<0.1 %; Orr et al., 2018)

alternatives_considered.chosen: surface sampling 0-12.5 m and bottom 12.5-17 m from day 29
alternatives_considered.alternatives: 0-10 m and 10-17 m layers used up to day 28
alternatives_considered.reason: deepening of the oxycline seen in CTD profiles

alternatives_considered.chosen: no gas-exchange tracer in the mesocosms
alternatives_considered.alternatives: N2O addition to monitor air-sea gas exchange; Wanninkhof (2014) equations
alternatives_considered.reason: N2O would interfere with 15N label incubations; Wanninkhof equations are not applicable to mesocosms

alternatives_considered.chosen: two OMZ-water treatments with four replicates each
alternatives_considered.alternatives: control mesocosms without OMZ water addition
alternatives_considered.reason: compromise to ensure enough replicates given the cost of mesocosm experimentation
